comparator.name: Communication Science
comparator.sourceNotes: The English and Dutch tracks share the Communication Science degree identity. The English track has ten 6 EC requirements in year one and eight 6 EC requirements plus two 6 EC restricted choices in year two. Year three combines 30 EC of open elective space, 6 EC each in Current Media Challenges and Philosophy of Science, and an 18 EC thesis. Current replacements in the transition table carry no extra credit. The language diagnostic and any required refresher are part of Project 1. Thesis entry requires Quantitative Research Methodology and 90 EC from years one and two. Students work in supervised research groups and submit individual assignments and a thesis. Assignments count for 40%, with the thesis assessed by a supervisor and second reader at 30% each. Attendance is compulsory and year-three mentorship must be completed before a thesis grade is awarded. Individual elective packages ordinarily require board approval and at least 12 EC at level 300.

alternatives.label: Communication, media and social research
alternatives.concept: Studies how messages influence audiences through rhetoric, media analysis and social psychology. Statistics and qualitative research support questions about audiences, and courses in leadership communication, consumer engagement and market research apply those methods and ideas to organizations.
alternatives.labelReason: The schedule integrates media, persuasion, audience psychology, organizational contexts and quantitative and qualitative methods.
progression: First-year courses introduce rhetoric, film, sociology and research design. Research Methods & Statistics precedes Statistics & Experimental Methods. Introductory and modern sociology precede advanced work on civil society. Rhetoric in Action follows the rhetoric foundation and takes place in the final spring. Entrepreneurship & Business Foundations precedes Market Research.

alternatives.label: Media, interpretation and public debate
alternatives.concept: Studies how film, television, digital media and public messages represent social issues. Climate communication and comparative politics provide contexts for public debate. Film adaptation and literary interpretation develop ways to read messages, while social research and statistics support empirical questions.
alternatives.labelReason: Four course substitutions shift business and organizational study toward comparative institutions, climate communication, film adaptation and interpretive perspectives; the label does not promise a technical digital-media degree.
alternatives.distinctness: Four courses (30 EC) differ in each direction. Comparative politics, climate communication, film adaptation and literary interpretation take the place of business foundations, consumer engagement, organizational psychology and market research.
progression: First-year courses introduce rhetoric, film, sociology and research design. Research Methods & Statistics precedes Statistics & Experimental Methods. Introductory and modern sociology precede advanced work on civil society. Rhetoric in Action follows the rhetoric foundation and takes place in the final spring.

selection.assessment: The closest option links rhetoric, persuasion, media, social psychology and empirical research to organizational and audience questions. Four substitutions shift the second option toward public debate and interpretation while preserving research methods. Health communication and platform analytics are real VU themes, but the available UCR courses do not support a third distinct option with sustained campaign or computational media work.

blocks: Both examine persuasion and audience influence. UCR studies framing, nudging, ethical persuasion and applied community communication; it is a partial relationship to VU marketing persuasion, not equal scope or credit.
Both address organizational communication, but UCR focuses on leadership models, ethics and emotional intelligence; it does not reproduce all VU organizational research.
Both study how people influence and respond to one another. UCR teaches social psychology broadly, while VU focuses on everyday interaction and communication skills.
UCR practises leadership communication and persuasion. VU requires a separate strategic communication project.
UCR studies leadership communication and, in the closest option, brand strategy. VU gives public relations and reputation management dedicated attention.
UCR applies persuasion in community projects. VU studies the design and effects of health communication campaigns.
Media, society and digital public life
UCR examines media representation. VU gives news selection, production and journalism research dedicated attention.
UCR develops empirical research and media interpretation in separate courses. VU combines them in a project on mediated reality.
UCR studies the development of sociological theory. VU traces the wider history of the social sciences.
UCR studies public spheres and media representation. VU focuses on how media, political actors and citizens influence each other in public debate.
UCR practises general data analysis in R. VU applies data methods in a dedicated social media analytics project.
UCR develops rhetorical, sociological and media perspectives across several courses. VU introduces communication science as a field in a dedicated course.
UCR practises experimental methods and applied persuasion in different courses. VU brings them together to test a communication intervention.
UCR studies changing media practices in several courses. VU examines current media challenges in a dedicated final-year course.
UCR analyzes film and television. VU studies media enjoyment and audience engagement as psychological processes.
Both include descriptive/inferential statistics and basic empirical study design; UCR adds a general group research project, without communication specialization.
UCR develops qualitative design, collection, interpretation and reflexivity; it is a partial methodological relationship, not the full VU social-research component.
Both cover multivariate models, regression, factor analysis and analysis of variance. UCR is general human-science statistics, without the VU communication-specific causal-design and R-lab sequence.

Both develop cleaning, analysis and visualization of data including text. UCR offers general data-science practice; VU additionally focuses on media content analysis in R and responsible LLM-based research, which this course does not reproduce.

notes.text: VU requires four communication projects, including a social media analytics project, plus specialist study in public relations and health campaigns and an empirical thesis. UCR develops related skills across separate courses. Check the language arrangements for the school-based work in Rhetoric in Action.

audience.programmeDescription: VU Communication Science studies how media and messages influence people, organizations and public life. This comparison uses its English-language route, with theoretical and empirical methods courses, four communication projects and a final empirical thesis.
audience.comparisonExplanation: UCR offers two ways to study messages and audiences. One emphasizes persuasion, leadership and market research. The other emphasizes media interpretation and public debate. Both include social research methods and statistics.

curriculum.limitation: The English-language pathway includes two restricted choices in year two and 30 EC of open study in year three. To start the 18 EC thesis, students must pass Quantitative Research Methodology and earn 90 EC in years one and two. Students conduct research in supervised groups and submit an individual thesis. Year-three mentorship is required before the thesis grade is awarded.

cellNotes.text: Both options practise data analysis in R. VU also teaches media content analysis and the research use of large language models.
